title: Pitch Invariance Reveals Skill-Specific Coordination in Human Movement: A Screw-Theoretic Reanalysis of Golf Swing Dynamics
content: This study reanalyzes a previously collected dataset of golf swing kinematics to investigate pitch—a screw-theoretic descriptor of motion—as a compact and robust invariant for skilled motor performance. Defined as the ratio of translational to rotational velocity along the instantaneous screw axis (ISA), pitch quantifies the dynamic coupling between biomechanical degrees of freedom. Synchronized time-series plots of pitch and vertical ground reaction force (GRF) were used to compare the performance of a proficient and a novice golfer. The proficient golfer demonstrated a narrow, stable pitch profile closely aligned with a single, well-timed GRF peak, indicating coherent rotational-translational coordination. In contrast, the novice golfer displayed erratic pitch fluctuations and temporally misaligned GRF patterns, revealing instability in movement organization. These results highlight pitch as a perceptual-motor invariant that captures the temporal structure of coordination, extending the relevance of screw theory as a diagnostic framework in human movement science.
